clinicalPearls: Mesenchymal tumour of fibroblastic type that can arise almost anywhere; classically pleural but frequently found in meninges, orbit, deep soft tissue, retroperitoneum and abdominal viscera.
Defined by a recurrent NAB2-STAT6 gene fusion, and nuclear STAT6 immunohistochemistry is a highly sensitive and specific diagnostic marker.
The old term haemangiopericytoma is now regarded as part of the solitary fibrous tumour spectrum rather than a separate entity.
Most behave in an indolent fashion, but all are considered to have malignant potential and a subset metastasises, so none is truly benign.
A minority secrete insulin-like growth factor 2 and cause non-islet-cell tumour hypoglycaemia (Doege-Potter syndrome), typically with large tumours.
Histology shows a patternless architecture of bland spindle cells, ropey collagen and prominent branching staghorn vessels; CD34 is usually positive.
Risk stratification uses patient age, tumour size, mitotic activity and necrosis to estimate the likelihood of recurrence and metastasis.
Complete surgical resection is the treatment of choice; late recurrence and distant spread can occur many years later, mandating prolonged follow-up.
reference.pathophysiology: Solitary fibrous tumour originates from a fibroblastic mesenchymal cell and is driven by a paracentric inversion on chromosome 12q that fuses the NAB2 and STAT6 genes. NAB2 is normally a transcriptional repressor of EGR1-responsive genes, but the fusion converts it into a transcriptional activator and drives constitutive expression of EGR1 target genes promoting proliferation and angiogenesis; the fusion protein also relocates STAT6 to the nucleus, the basis of the diagnostic immunostain. Different NAB2-STAT6 breakpoint variants correlate loosely with clinical behaviour, some being associated with the more cellular, aggressive phenotype. The characteristic branching haemangiopericytoma-like vasculature reflects the strong angiogenic drive. A subset of tumours aberrantly produces incompletely processed insulin-like growth factor 2, which activates insulin receptors and causes refractory hypoglycaemia (Doege-Potter syndrome). Progression to frankly malignant, dedifferentiated tumours is associated with additional genetic hits such as TERT promoter mutations and TP53 alterations, correlating with higher mitotic counts, necrosis and metastatic potential.
additionalInvestigations: Contrast-enhanced CT or MRI of the primary site to characterise vascularity and resectability
Core needle biopsy with histological assessment of mitoses and necrosis
Molecular confirmation of NAB2-STAT6 fusion where diagnosis is uncertain
Fasting glucose and paired insulin / C-peptide with IGF-2 assessment if hypoglycaemic symptoms occur
Staging CT of the chest for suspected malignant or metastatic tumours
Long-term surveillance imaging because of the risk of late recurrence
redFlags: Rapid tumour growth, increasing mitotic activity or necrosis on pathology
Symptomatic hypoglycaemia suggesting a large IGF-2-secreting tumour
New or progressive neurological deficit from an intracranial or spinal lesion
Development of pulmonary or other distant metastases
Recurrence at the resection site during follow-up
reference.prognosis: Most tumours are cured by complete resection, but outcome depends on validated risk factors (age, size, mitotic rate and necrosis); high-risk and dedifferentiated tumours carry a meaningful risk of late local recurrence and distant metastasis. Lifelong follow-up is advised because relapses may appear a decade or more after surgery.
pitfalls: Assuming the tumour is benign; all solitary fibrous tumours retain malignant potential and require follow-up.
Missing Doege-Potter hypoglycaemia by not linking a large tumour to unexplained low glucose.
Relying on the outdated haemangiopericytoma label as though it were a distinct diagnosis.
Overlooking dedifferentiation, where a high-grade sarcomatous component may lose CD34 expression.
Incomplete or piecemeal resection that leaves positive margins and predisposes to recurrence.
references: WHO Classification of Soft Tissue and Bone Tumours
WHO Classification of Tumours of the Central Nervous System (for meningeal lesions)
management: Treat solitary fibrous tumour, including the older haemangiopericytoma diagnosis, as one entity managed like a fibroblastic soft tissue sarcoma, with intent set by resectability and histologic risk rather than a fixed stage
Complete surgical resection is the treatment of choice for localised disease at any site, deep soft tissue, retroperitoneum, meninges, or pleura
For pleural disease, tailor resection to growth pattern, pedunculated tumours have a better prognosis, and complete resection should remove the tumour, its pedicle, and the site of origin
Perform en bloc resection of adjacent lung, chest wall, or diaphragm when needed to achieve complete resection of pleural disease
Offer re-excision as the treatment of choice for local recurrence, since long-term survival remains possible after re-excision
Use tumour size above 10 cm and mitotic rate above 4 per 10 high-power fields, along with age and necrosis based risk models, to stratify metastatic risk
Recognise that retroperitoneal disease carries a notably worse prognosis than disease at other sites
Discuss suspected or confirmed cases in a multidisciplinary sarcoma tumour board to guide surgery, radiotherapy, and follow-up intensity
Consider postoperative radiotherapy for positive margins or high-risk histology, individualised by the sarcoma multidisciplinary team, following general soft tissue sarcoma practice

For unresectable or metastatic disease, favour a trial of an antiangiogenic tyrosine kinase inhibitor such as sunitinib or sorafenib over anthracycline based chemotherapy, since these tumours respond poorly to anthracyclines, guided by sarcoma specialist input

Watch for Doege-Potter syndrome, paraneoplastic non-islet-cell hypoglycaemia from aberrant insulin-like growth factor 2, mainly in large tumours, and manage it with correction of hypoglycaemia and definitive tumour resection alongside endocrine input
Plan prolonged surveillance imaging of the primary site and chest, since late local recurrence and late distant metastasis can occur even after apparently complete resection

Refer to a sarcoma specialist centre or multidisciplinary team for high-risk features such as large size, elevated mitotic rate, retroperitoneal location, incomplete resection, or malignant or dedifferentiated histology

Refer pleural disease with broad-based growth, suspected chest wall, lung, or diaphragmatic involvement, or recurrence to a thoracic surgical team experienced in en bloc resection, and refer new hypoglycaemia in a patient with a known large tumour urgently for endocrine and oncology assessment
